Gemini subscription

Google AI Ultra subscription inference through Antigravity CLI (Gemini 4 Neon, Carbon, Argon, Hydrogen) or the official Gemini CLI: one live ACP session per conversation, a private Gemini home, managed settings, tool handoff and the fail-closed checks around each.

About 21 min read · 8 sections

On this page
01 Why the environment is the first line of defence 02 Live sessions 03 Tools: the CLI is an inference backend only 04 Permissions 05 Prompt framing 06 Sign in 07 Antigravity CLI 08 Continuation, usage and failures

Use "geminiCli": "antigravity" for a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription. On 18 June 2026 Google stopped serving the Gemini CLI for Pro and Ultra accounts and moved them to Antigravity CLI (agy). The Gemini 4 models reach a subscription only there. See Antigravity CLI. The rest of this page describes the Gemini CLI backend, which stays the default for existing configurations.

A gemini-subscription provider spends a Google AI Ultra subscription through the official Gemini CLI (gemini). API keys are never used: every GEMINI_*, GOOGLE_*, VERTEX* and OTEL_* variable is removed from the CLI's environment before it starts, and the CLI signs in once into the gateway's own private home. Model choices are never changed automatically.

The session mechanics are shared with Grok sessions: one long-lived CLI process per conversation, ACP over stdio, caller tools as held calls on a loopback MCP endpoint. Grok refuses a conversation it cannot continue; Gemini replays it by default (see resume below). This page covers what is specific to the Gemini CLI, and the two places where it is stricter than Grok.

Codex ──request──▶ gateway ──ACP (ndjson over stdio)──▶ gemini --acp -m <model>
                      │  ▲                                    │ MCP over loopback HTTP
                      │  └── tools/call held open ◀───────────┘ http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/<token>
                      └─ yields {tool call, done}; next request answers the held call

Why the environment is the first line of defence

Two findings from probing CLI 0.70.0 drive most of this provider's design:

  • An ambient GEMINI_API_KEY silently wins. With the inherited environment the CLI answered a session/new using API-key billing; with a clean environment the same call failed with "Gemini API key is missing or not configured." ADC (GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS), GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_*, GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL, GOOGLE_CLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN, GEMINI_CLI_AUTH_OVERRIDE and GEMINI_MODEL do the same kind of silent substitution. So geminiEnv deletes every GEMINI_*, GOOGLE_*, VERTEX* and OTEL_* variable and the few outside those families that still change what the CLI is (CLOUD_SHELL, SANDBOX, VITEST, NO_BROWSER, and the variables that make it skip the browser: CI, DEBIAN_FRONTEND, BROWSER, SSH_CONNECTION), then sets only the five it owns.
  • Credentials go to the macOS keychain unless told otherwise. GEMINI_FORCE_FILE_STORAGE=true keeps the sign-in in <home>/.gemini/oauth_creds.json (mode 0600) instead of the keychain. GEMINI_FORCE_ENCRYPTED_FILE_STORAGE must stay unset: when set, the CLI imports and deletes oauth_creds.json and moves the credential to the keychain.

GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_SETTINGS_PATH and GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_DEFAULTS_PATH both point at names the gateway never creates inside the home, which closes the machine-wide scope rather than competing with it. System settings outrank the home's own settings.json and system defaults outrank those, so a /Library/Application Support/GeminiCli document could reopen anything the managed document closes; each variable replaces its path outright, so naming an absent file leaves that scope with nothing to load. (A file that does exist is also refused unless root owns it, which nothing inside this home can be.) What remains is <home>/.gemini/settings.json — the user scope, rewritten before every spawn — as the only settings document the CLI acts on. GEMINI_CLI_NO_RELAUNCH=true keeps one process, so one SIGKILL to the process group ends the CLI and anything it started.

Live sessions

geminiSessions is optional and validated exactly like grokSessions:

{ "id": "gemini", "type": "gemini-subscription", "geminiSessions": { "mode": "live", "max": 4, "parkMinutes": 30, "toolWaitMinutes": 25, "resume": "replay" } }
Field Range Default Meaning
mode live, oneshot live oneshot is refused: the Gemini CLI has no standalone transport here
max 1–16 4 Live conversations at once. A newcomer past the cap is refused (capacity); no session is evicted
parkMinutes 5–240 30 A session idle after a finished turn is closed
toolWaitMinutes 1–25 25 A session waiting for tool outputs is closed (never longer than parkMinutes)
resume replay, refuse replay What happens to a conversation whose session ended or does not hold its history

Resume. A conversation can lose its session: it sat idle past parkMinutes, the gateway restarted, it started on another model and switched to Gemini, or its history changed (an edit or a compaction). With replay, the gateway closes any session that no longer matches, reopens the conversation's ended-session record, and starts a new CLI whose first prompt is the whole conversation. That turn pays for the full history again and takes as long as a first turn; later turns continue the new session normally. Telemetry records the spawn with replayed: <reason> (parked, session_missing, prefix_diverged, ...). With refuse, the conversation stays closed and the client gets session_continuity_unavailable, whose message says to start a new chat. concurrent and capacity are refused in both modes, and a session another gateway process still holds is never taken over.

Start time. Every spawned record carries startMs, the time from launching the CLI to its session being ready, so a slow first turn can be split into CLI start-up and the model's own time to first output (firstEventMs on request_completed).

Process. gemini --acp -m <model>, started in a private 0700 scratch folder which is also the session/new cwd — the CLI creates storage for both its boot cwd and the session cwd, so a mismatch would make the gateway's own repository a "project" in that home. Each process also gets its own disposable GEMINI_CLI_HOME inside that folder (see Transcripts). The gateway speaks ACP: initialize (advertising clientCapabilities fs/terminal off), session/new with exactly one http MCP server named gateway, session/prompt, and it answers every agent request itself; anything but a permission request gets JSON-RPC -32601. notifications/initialized is never sent (the CLI rejects it), and the CLI implements no ACP extension methods, so no method prefix has an excusable params: null. No approval, yolo or auto-approve flag is ever passed. There is no reasoning-effort flag, so effort travels in the caller's own instructions.

Requests with no conversation id. A request that carries neither a thread nor a session id has no conversation to come back to, so it follows Grok's one-shot rule: it is served by a fresh process, and that session is closed as soon as its turn completes. It is never parked and never counts against max afterwards, so any number of anonymous text requests in a row succeed. A turn that ends in tool calls still hands them to the client, but the continuation (the same history plus the tool outputs, again with no id) cannot be joined to anything: it is a new, unnamed conversation with history, and is refused before a CLI starts as session_continuity_unavailable / session_missing. The alternative, refusing anonymous requests that offer tools up front, was rejected because it would also refuse the many requests that offer tools and never use them.

System prompt. The CLI has no system-prompt field on session/new. The gateway's instructions — its own system text plus the caller's leading instructions — are written to a 0600 file in the session folder and named by GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD. One process per conversation means the file is written once and stays immutable, which is what the CLI requires: it re-reads that file on every prompt turn.

Models. Selection comes from -m, which the gateway always passes; GEMINI_MODEL is stripped and model.name is pinned in the managed settings, so the CLI never routes a pro versus flash turn on its own. A text-only catalog for an Ultra subscription:

{ "id": "gemini", "type": "gemini-subscription", "label": "Gemini",
  "models": { "gemini/gemini-3.8-flash": "gemini-3.8-flash" },
  "modelMetadata": { "gemini/gemini-3.8-flash": { "displayName": "Gemini 3.8 Flash", "contextWindow": 1048576, "inputModalities": ["text"] } } }

gemini/gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini/gemini-3-pro-preview, gemini/gemini-2.5-pro, gemini/gemini-3.8-flash, gemini/gemini-3.5-flash, gemini/gemini-3.5-flash-lite and gemini/gemini-3-flash-preview are the expected Ultra ids at 1,048,576 tokens. Do not configure gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools: that id is offered only for API-key auth. Availability is entitlement-gated, so re-check the list against the CLI after a real Ultra login. Images are refused before any CLI starts (promptCapabilities advertises them, but the gateway accepts text only).

Tools: the CLI is an inference backend only

There is no single "disable all tools" switch, and two mechanisms are needed because they do different jobs.

geminiManagedPolicy() writes <home>/.gemini/policies/gateway.toml, which the CLI loads at its user tier — above workspace, extension and the bundled defaults. A rule's rank is tier + priority/1000 and the highest matching rule decides, so this file is the only thing that outranks the CLI's bundled default policies, which allow read_file, glob, grep_search, list_directory, google_web_search, codebase_investigator, cli_help, get_internal_docs and the tracker tools with no permission request at all, and let agents.toml allow invoke_agent. It holds three rules: mcp_gateway_* → ask_user (priority 999), the built-ins by name → deny (900), and * → deny (800). The ask rule must outrank the denies, because a deny-all on its own would swallow the caller's tools too — the CLI names one mcp_gateway_<tool>. Nothing here ever answers allow; the gateway's own permission reply is the only thing that lets a tool run.

tools.exclude names the same built-ins (geminiBuiltInTools) and is not redundant: an excluded tool is also dropped from the CLI's registry (isActiveTool), so the model is never offered it, where a deny rule alone would still advertise it.

  • tools.core: [] is not usable as a shortcut: its wildcard DENY also matches mcp_gateway_* and would kill the caller's own tools.
  • mcpServers is {} and mcp.serverCommand is absent — session/new merges the settings' servers with the caller's, and a stdio entry would let the CLI spawn a process.
  • mcp.allowed and --allowed-mcp-server-names are deliberately unset. Both generate an ALLOW policy rule for mcp_gateway_*, which would run every caller tool with no session/request_permission; leaving them alone is what keeps Grok parity and defence in depth. Same for mcpServers[*].trust.
  • security.disableAlwaysAllow, disableYoloMode, enablePermanentToolApproval: false and admin.secureModeEnabled remove always-allow and YOLO.
  • Telemetry, usage statistics, auto-update, checkpointing, worktrees (a startup git rev-parse), extensions, skills, hooks, IDE, agents, memory and discoveryMaxDirs are all off, and advanced.ignoreLocalEnv is true.

Transcripts never reach the persistent home

The CLI records every conversation: ChatRecordingService is constructed unconditionally and writes <home>/.gemini/tmp/<project>/chats/session-*.jsonl with the full prompt text, plus <home>/.gemini/history/, and 0.70.0 has no setting, flag or environment variable that turns that off (general.sessionRetention.enabled: false only stops it cleaning up old files). So the persistent Gemini home never runs the CLI. Each live process gets its own disposable home, <session folder>/home, a 0700 directory holding only:

  • the managed settings.json and policies/gateway.toml (0600), written fresh;
  • a 0600 copy of oauth_creds.json, and google_accounts.json when it exists.

When the session ends the process is killed first, then the credential is carried back if it changed (the CLI refreshes its access token while it runs) and the whole folder is deleted, so the transcript dies with the session. The copy-back runs under the same cross-process lock as the other private files (withPrivateFileLock on oauth_creds.json), writes atomically at 0600, and is deliberately cautious:

Case Result
Credential unchanged Nothing is written
Credential refreshed and the persistent copy is still what was handed out Copied back
Persistent copy changed meanwhile (a newer sign-in, another session's refresh) The persistent copy wins
Disposable copy no longer has both tokens Never replaces a good credential

A gateway that exits (process.exit, including during startup or a sign-in) is covered by a synchronous exit hook (src/providers/exit-cleanup.ts). Each session and each sign-in registers it the moment it acquires something, not when startup finishes: first the scratch folder, then the CLI's process group. At exit the group is killed and the folder (with the copied credential) is removed; the copy-back is skipped, which only loses a refresh the next request repeats. A gateway that was killed outright (SIGKILL, a crash) runs no hook, so every scratch root records its owner (owner.json: pid, boot id, process start) and the first session or sign-in of the next gateway run removes gateway-gemini-live-* and gateway-gemini-login-* roots whose owner is gone, from an earlier boot, or a reused pid. The sweep never touches a root with no owner record or a live owner, and removes folders only: an orphaned ACP CLI ends when its stdin closes, and a sign-in CLI gives up after its own five minutes. The persistent home receives tmp/ or history/ from no inference path; src/tests/gemini-home-isolation.test.ts fails if it ever does. The persistent home's own settings.json and policies/gateway.toml are still written, but only as a managed reference: the CLI reads the per-session copies.

The CLI never opens a browser during inference

With selectedType: oauth-personal and a credential the CLI cannot refresh (revoked or expired beyond use), the CLI's boot calls refreshAuth before it answers initialize, falls into its browser sign-in and opens a tab. A missing refresh_token is caught before anything starts (a 401, below), but a revoked one only fails inside the CLI. Findings from 0.70.0 that decide the mechanism:

  • NO_BROWSER is unusable: ACP counts as interactive, so the CLI would print an alternate screen and a code prompt on stdout and read the code from stdin, the protocol stream (observed: it took our initialize request as the authorization code). The same happens with CI, DEBIAN_FRONTEND, BROWSER=www-browser or SSH_CONNECTION (on macOS), which shouldAttemptBrowserLaunch treats as "no browser". All of them are removed from the CLI's environment.
  • The browser is opened by childProcess.spawn("open", [url]) (xdg-open on Linux), by name. Each session folder therefore holds a bin/ with stand-in open and xdg-open scripts, first on the CLI's PATH. A stand-in creates browser-requested in the session folder and exits 0; nothing is launched.
  • While initialize and session/new are pending the gateway polls for that marker. When it appears the CLI is killed and the request fails at once with HTTP 401 authentication and a fixed message (Gemini's saved Google sign-in can no longer be used. Run gateway login gemini or use Reconnect in the app.); the CLI's text and the URL never reach the caller. The conversation's reservation is released, so signing in and repeating the request works.

Verified against the real binary with a bogus credential: initialize is never answered, open is called with an https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth URL, and the request is a 401 in under two seconds (GATEWAY_TEST_REAL_GEMINI=1, src/tests/gemini-real-cli.test.ts). On Linux the CLI only tries a browser when DISPLAY, WAYLAND_DISPLAY or MIR_SOCKET is set, so the gateway sets DISPLAY=:0 when none is; the stand-in makes the value harmless. That Linux path is not verified against a real CLI.

The policy file is loaded by the CLI

<home>/.gemini/policies/gateway.toml is read by the bundle's loadPoliciesFromToml, which silently drops a file it cannot parse: the CLI then runs on its bundled defaults, which allow read_file, glob, google_web_search and invoke_agent without a prompt. The loader returns errors as data (errorType toml_parse or schema_validation; unknown tool names come back as warnings) and the CLI only prints them, so stderr is not a reliable channel. src/tests/gemini-real-cli.test.ts calls the real loader from the installed bundle: the gateway's file loads with no error and no warning, every rule is present, and PolicyEngine answers ask_user for mcp_gateway_* and deny for the built-ins, run_shell_command and any other server; a malformed or schema-invalid copy reports its error and loads zero rules, after which read_file is allow. The same check showed the bundle's real shell tool is run_shell_command (plus tracker_visualize and complete_task), which the first list lacked; geminiBuiltInTools now names them.

Announcement guard. A session/update tool_call or tool_call_update that names a native built-in, a tool kind such as execute, a server other than gateway, or a running or completed tool that is not in the caller's catalog ends the session at once (invalid_tool_call). Built-in or caller tool is decided from the CLI's structured identities, never from ACP's title: a tool the CLI's own _meta["gemini-cli"].mcp identifies as a call of the gateway server whose tool is in the caller's catalog is the caller's tool even when it is named grep_search, read_file, glob or list_directory, because a caller may choose those names and the CLI's _meta block is not text the model shapes. The title names a tool only where the frame carries no structured identity at all — there nothing else distinguishes one of the CLI's own tools, and for the auto-allowed built-ins no permission request would ever arrive to refuse it. An announcement that names nothing at all is left to the permission layer, because closing a session throws away a conversation whose history cannot be replayed.

MCP naming. The CLI names MCP tools mcp_<server>_<tool> (mcp_gateway_<tool>) and carries the real server and tool name for an MCP call under toolCall._meta["gemini-cli"].mcp. Both spellings are consulted.

Permissions

Every session/request_permission is answered by the gateway. What is judged is the tool the CLI's own structured fields name — toolCall._meta["gemini-cli"].mcp first, then a structured name or rawInput.tool_name, each also read with the mcp_gateway_ prefix stripped. The display title never authorizes a run: it is free text the model shaped, and one shaped to a caller tool's name would otherwise make a native tool look like one of the caller's, so a request with no structured identity in the catalog is refused. The request's own optionId is echoed back verbatim.

Request Answer
A tool named by the CLI's structured fields as the gateway server's and in this session's caller catalog allow_once (ProceedOnce)
Anything else (native tool, unknown tool, other server, titled only, unidentifiable) reject_once (Cancel), else cancelled

allow_always (ProceedAlwaysServer, ProceedAlwaysTool, ProceedAlwaysAndSave) is never selected — the CLI persists a policy rule for such an answer — and security.disableAlwaysAllow keeps those options from being offered at all. A session denied 25 times is closed. The client, never the provider, executes tools.

Prompt framing

A hazard Grok does not have: Session.prompt concatenates the leading text parts and, if the result begins with / or $, runs it as one of the CLI's own commands instead of answering it — /extensions install <git url> installs and runs code, and the turn comes back as a believable zero-usage end_turn. Every prompt is therefore prefixed with a fixed framing line that starts with an ordinary character, so a caller prompt that begins with / stays data to answer. The continuation ledger is keyed on the caller's history, not on this text, so framing cannot make a later request look like a different conversation.

Sign in

The gateway keeps its own home, <stateDirectory>/gemini-home unless geminiHome names another directory, private at 0700, with settings.json and the managed system-settings file at 0600. Sign it in once per Mac:

gateway login gemini

The desktop app's Reconnect runs the same flow (src/providers/gemini-login.ts). There is no login subcommand and no device-code flow: run with nothing to do, the CLI starts the Google browser flow, which the managed settings pin (security.auth.selectedType/enforcedType = oauth-personal). What the real 0.70.0 binary does without a terminal, probed against it:

  1. It prints Opening authentication page in your browser. Do you want to continue? [Y/n]: and reads the answer from stdin. With stdin closed (the old Reconnect) nothing is ever answered, the process exits 0 with no credential, and no URL appears.
  2. On Y it runs the browser opener by name with the sign-in URL. It prints no URL of its own.

So the helper (a Reconnect click or the gateway login gemini command is the consent) writes Y\n when the question appears, captures the URL through the same stand-in open described above, and opens it itself, once, only when it is an https://accounts.google.com/ URL (the command also prints it). It stops the CLI once the sign-in has finished, or after six minutes, or on cancel. The CLI's callback handler saves the tokens first, then fetches and caches the Google account (google_accounts.json), and only then redirects the browser to its success page. So after the credential appears the helper waits until the account is cached plus one second for the redirect, or the CLI exits, for at most 15 seconds. Stopping on the credential alone left the account uncached and showed "127.0.0.1 refused to connect" in the browser although the sign-in had worked. The callback is served on 127.0.0.1 of the computer that runs the login, so approve the sign-in in a browser on that same computer. Two rules matter:

  • Success is the credential, never the exit code. The file must exist in the CLI's home: oauth_creds.json, parsed, carrying both access_token and refresh_token. A clean exit without it fails; a failing exit after it succeeds.
  • The login CLI is isolated. It runs with its working directory set to an empty private folder, never the caller's: a trusted workspace's .gemini/settings.json or .env must not reach a process that holds a Google sign-in. It also runs in a disposable home like a session, and the credential is installed into the persistent home only after it is verified. The gateway never creates <home>/.env or <home>/.gemini/.env, and refuses to start the CLI (login or inference, HTTP 400) while either exists, because the CLI would load it ahead of the managed settings and an auth variable in it would win.

Never answer ACP authenticate on a live session: for oauth-personal it refreshes the sign-in and, on a mismatch, deletes the stored credential. The gateway never calls it, and initialize also advertises a gateway auth method that could inject a custom base URL; that is never used either.

A home that is not signed in (no credential, or no refresh_token) fails the request with HTTP 401 authentication before the CLI starts, and a credential that exists but cannot refresh is caught at boot as described above, so inference can never open a browser or block before any JSON-RPC.

Antigravity CLI

With "geminiCli": "antigravity" the same provider runs agy acp (Antigravity CLI, checked with 1.5.14 on a Google AI Ultra account) instead of gemini --acp. The live-session mechanics above are unchanged: one process per conversation, caller tools as held calls on the loopback MCP endpoint, and refusal rather than replay.

{ "id": "gemini", "type": "gemini-subscription", "label": "Gemini", "geminiCli": "antigravity",
  "models": { "gemini/gemini-4-neon": "gemini-4-neon", "gemini/gemini-4-hydrogen": "gemini-4-hydrogen" },
  "modelMetadata": { "gemini/gemini-4-neon": { "displayName": "Gemini 4 Neon", "contextWindow": 1048576,
    "inputModalities": ["text"], "reasoningEfforts": ["low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"] } } }

Install and sign in. Install with brew install --cask antigravity-cli (Homebrew then owns updates), then run gateway login gemini in a terminal. It runs agy acp --login with HOME set to the gateway's Gemini home: it prints a Google sign-in link, and you paste back the code the browser shows, so it also works over SSH. The sign-in is saved as <home>/.gemini/antigravity-cli/antigravity-oauth-token (0600). The app cannot run this sign-in because it needs a terminal, so its Reconnect button is hidden for this backend.

Models. An Ultra account lists gemini-4-neon, gemini-4-carbon, gemini-4-argon, gemini-4-hydrogen, the orchestrators gemini-pro-orchestrator, gemini-pro-orchestrator-neon and gemini-pro-orchestrator-argon, and gemini-3.8-flash. agy acp has no model flag. After session/new, the session sets model, mode (default) and, when the caller chose a supported effort, thought_level (low, medium, high, xhigh) with session/set_config_option. The session refuses to start when the CLI does not report the requested value as current, so an unavailable model is never swapped for another one. The gateway's instructions travel as _meta.antigravity.systemPrompt.append on session/new.

Private home. agy keeps its sign-in, settings and a record of every conversation under $HOME/.gemini/antigravity-cli/. Each process runs with HOME set to a disposable folder inside its session folder. That folder holds the managed settings.json, the tool hook, an empty ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json, and 0600 copies of the sign-in and installation_id. A token the CLI refreshed is carried back when the session ends, unless a newer sign-in replaced the copy that was handed out. The CLI's environment is only HOME, PATH, TMPDIR, USER, LOGNAME and the locale, so no API key or Google Cloud credential can switch it off the subscription.

Native tools. agy has its own shell, file, web, image, scheduling and subagent tools, and agy acp has no flag that removes them. Three layers keep them off:

Layer What it does
PreToolUse hook (antigravity-hook.ts) Runs before every tool call. It denies every tool except mcp_gateway_* and reads of the cached gateway schemas, and a denied call never starts. allow only passes the call on to the permission request below.
Permission requests (antigravity-acp.ts) toolPermission: "strict" makes file and shell actions ask the gateway, which answers as in the next table.
Completed-call guard A native tool reported completed ends the session.

The hook exists because permissions are not enough. With 1.5.14 in strict, search_web and invoke_subagent ran without any permission request, and 2.2.3, which had no hook, could only end the session afterwards. The hook fails closed: when its command crashed or did not exist, the CLI refused the call. A broken hook therefore also stops the caller's tools. The hook script and hooks.json are written into each session's own ~/.gemini/config/.

The managed settings also set agentMode to the standard mode (never auto, which approves "safe" commands itself), keep useG1Credits off so AI credits are never spent after the plan's quota runs out, and deny every command, write and URL action. The deny rules are an extra layer only: with 1.5.14, agy sometimes asked for a denied command instead of refusing it.

The gateway answers every permission request (antigravity-acp.ts):

Request Answer
mcp_gateway_<tool> for a tool in this session's caller catalog allow_once
read_file of a schema the CLI cached from the gateway's own MCP server (<session>/home/.gemini/antigravity-cli/mcp/gateway/<file>) allow_once
Anything else reject_once, so the model continues without it

The CLI caches MCP tool schemas on disk and the model sometimes reads one with read_file before calling the tool, which is why that one native read is allowed. Every call is announced in_progress before the hook runs, and a refused call ends failed. A native tool reported completed therefore means the CLI ran something of its own, and the session ends with invalid_tool_call.

Prompts are framed like the Gemini CLI's, because agy also runs a prompt that starts with / as one of its own commands (/schedule, /teamwork, /browser).

Continuation, usage and failures

Continuation, the ended-record store, refusal codes and cancellation follow Grok sessions unchanged — they are the shared implementation in src/providers/acp-*.ts. A request continues its conversation's process only when its history is exactly what the session holds plus the new items; anything else, and any request for a conversation whose session already ended, is a final 400 session_continuity_unavailable, never a replay. gemini_session telemetry carries outcome, a fixed missReason (src/providers/gemini-reasons.ts) and counts; no tokens, request bodies, tool arguments or environment values are logged.

Usage arrives twice: a usage_update session/update per finished turn, and on the prompt result as {inputTokens, outputTokens, cachedReadTokens, thoughtTokens, totalTokens} plus per-model _meta.quota.model_usage. There is no cost field, unlike Grok's costUsd.

Failures are mapped to fixed classes and provider prose is never forwarded: a rejected sign-in (the CLI's -32000 on session/new, or a 401/403) is HTTP 401 authentication; a 429, a quota or an exhausted-allowance report is HTTP 429 rate_limit_exceeded; a billing problem is insufficient_quota; overload is 503. A failure after the prompt was sent is final (session_dead), not a retryable 502.

Not yet verified against a real Ultra login: the entitlement-gated model list, and exactly how quota and rate-limit failures surface, so the 401-versus-502 mapping above is built on fixed patterns rather than observed payloads. Re-check both after a real login.
